title: New Data on the Chaining of Children and Teens
author: Peter Gray
summary: Peter Gray presents data from a new Institute for Family Studies survey of nearly 24,000 U.S. parents covering over 40,000 children, revealing that American children have drastically less outdoor freedom than previous generations. Fourteen-year-olds today have less freedom than 5-year-olds had a few decades ago. The data show that 58% of 10-year-olds, 27% of 14-year-olds, and 16% of 17-year-olds cannot leave their own yard without adult accompaniment. Remarkably, 62% of surveyed parents said children aged 8-12 should receive MORE supervision than they currently do -- even as most 10-year-olds are already confined to their own yard. Gray argues this level of restriction is both irrational and cruel, and that a primary effect of restricted movement is the loss of opportunity to socialize with peers outside of adult-structured settings. The findings hold across neighborhood type and socioeconomic class, suggesting this is a broad cultural phenomenon rather than a response to actual safety data.
points: * Survey data from nearly 24,000 U.S. parents shows that 58% of 10-year-olds and 27% of 14-year-olds cannot leave their own yard without adult accompaniment -- a level of restriction unthinkable a generation ago. * The restrictions are not correlated with actual neighborhood safety: children in EPA-rated 'walkable' neighborhoods are just as restricted as those in less walkable areas, and findings hold across socioeconomic groups. * The primary measurable effect of restricted movement is reduced time spent with other children outside of adult-controlled activities, which has downstream consequences for social development and friendship formation. * Perhaps most alarming: 62% of parents said children aged 8-12 should receive more supervision than they already do -- even as data show most 10-year-olds cannot leave their own yard without adult escort. * Gray frames this as both a societal failure (the 'chaining' metaphor) and a developmental crisis, citing previous work on how the loss of free-range childhood has damaged children's psychological and social growth.
quotes: I have seen data like these before, so I should not be shocked. But every time I read of a new survey showing how restricted American children are I'm shocked again.
Looking just at the second data column, 58% of 10-year-olds, 27% of 14-year-olds, and 16% of 17-year-olds cannot leave their own yard without adult accompaniment.

Remarkably, in the same survey, 62% of parents said that children in the 8 to 12-year-old range should receive more supervision than they currently do! It's hard to imagine how that would even be possible, when 58% of 10-year-olds are not allowed to leave their own yard without an adult guard.

The study further showed that these data are very little affected by the nature of the neighborhood or the socioeconomic class of the respondents. Children and teens in neighborhoods rated by the EPA as highly 'walkable' were just as restricted in movement as those in neighborhoods rated as less walkable.

Regardless of age, the primary variable affecting children's time spent with other children, outside of school or other adult-controlled activities, was their degree of freedom to travel away from home on their own.
